In Chapter 14 we introduced the general logic of ANOVA and used its independent-samples variant to analyze data from a between-participants design. But like the $t$ test, ANOVA has different varieties that can be applied in different situations. In this chapter we'll introduce the **related-samples ANOVA**. Just like the related-samples $t$ test, this is for use with within-participants or matched-subjects designs. For a within-participants design with one factor, you'll also see it called a **one-way repeated-measures ANOVA**. The logic of $F$ is the same; what's new is how we account for differences between people.

## Repeated measures, repeated

We spent Chapter 13 looking at data from a handful of kids who had completed a racing game twice, first alone and then in competition with another kid. We used a related-samples $t$ test to compare the two times via difference scores. The kids were generally a little faster in their second race, the one they did head-to-head with a rival. But we left a loose end. Was it the competition that spurred them to race quicker, or was it just practice at turning the reel? With just the two races from each kid to compare, we couldn't tell.

What would another race tell us? If the kids raced alone twice before competing, we could see how much they improved before a competitor entered the picture. That would give us more information about practice, though it still wouldn't tell us how much further practice alone would have helped on the third trial.

In fact, Norman Triplett gave each child six timed trials, with different sequences of solo and competition trials [@triplett1898dynamogenic]. Here we'll use the first three trials from five children who all followed the same order: alone, alone, then competition.

@tbl-related-anova-data shows their times. These are different children from the five in Chapter 13. (As before, I cherry-picked them from the children Triplett classified as positively stimulated to make a useful teaching example, and rounded their times to whole seconds. This isn't a full reanalysis of Triplett's data.)

| Child | First alone | Second alone | Competition |
|:------|--:|--:|--:|
| Stephen M. | 51 | 50 | 43 |
| Mary W. | 56 | 53 | 46 |
| Bertha A. | 56 | 49 | 48 |
| Clyde G. | 36 | 35 | 32 |
| Lucile W. | 52 | 50 | 43 |
| $M$ | 50.20 | 47.40 | 42.40 |
| $SS$ | 272.80 | 201.20 | 153.20 |

: Times (in seconds) for five children from Triplett's study. The columns follow the order of their first three trials. {#tbl-related-anova-data}

Now we have two alone times from each racer to compare, giving us an indication of improvement with practice. And we can compare competition with the second time alone. Competition always comes last in this example, so that comparison still mixes competition with further practice. We'll return to that limitation when we interpret the results.

How do we analyze all three conditions? With two, we simply subtracted each child's pair of times to get one difference score. Here there are three scores per kid, so subtraction can't handle the whole set of scores in a single test. But you know what can: ANOVA. The only difference between this and what we did in Chapter 14 is the relatedness of the samples. But how can we extend the logic of ANOVA to capture and set aside the differences between children that the related-samples $t$ test removed?

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-third-condition.qmd >}}

## Partitioning variance in related samples

Let's think about this in terms of partitioning the variability in the data. In Chapter 14 we split the total sum of squares into between-groups and within-groups components. Any treatment effect contributes to differences between groups, while chance contributes both between and within groups. Dividing each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom gives the two mean squares for $F$.

{{< interactive-figure relatedRecapPartitionDiagram makeVariancePartitionDiagram options='{"preset":"independent-detailed","formula":false,"ariaLabel":"Diagram partitioning total variability into variance between groups, which contains any treatment effect, sampling error, and individual differences, and variance within groups, which contains sampling error and individual differences."}' fallback="Diagram partitioning total variability into variance between groups, which contains any treatment effect, sampling error, and individual differences, and variance within groups, which contains sampling error and individual differences." >}}

The diagram makes one source of that chance variability explicit: individual differences. Notice that Clyde demolished the other kids' times. Having one child who's much faster than the others adds a substantial amount of variability within each condition. But Clyde appears in every condition, so his generally faster pace doesn't explain the differences between them.

### Removing individual differences

<!-- With the related-samples ANOVA, we start out the same, partitioning the total variance into variance between groups and variance within groups. Any treatment effect still contributes to variance between groups and not within groups. Sampling error still contributes to both differences between and within groups. But like I said, individual differences are eliminated as a potential source of variability between groups by virtue of the design — it's the same people or matched subjects in each group. So the individuals do not differ between groups. But of course, they do still differ within groups. So individual differences are a potential source of within-group variance.

So if we use the same numerator and denominator here as for the independent-samples ANOVA, the ratio wouldn't be balanced anymore. We'd have treatment plus error in the numerator and error plus individual differences in the denominator. So those different sources of variability would contribute differently to the numerator and denominator and wouldn't cancel out nicely in the ratio like they did before.

This would be a problem. And so with related samples, we have a little extra work to do, because, happily, we can partition out the variance in the denominator, separating the sampling error and the individual differences. We will partition that within-group variance into two components: error variance, labeled $MS_{\text{error}}$, and between-people variance, $MS_{\text{people}}$. As the name suggests, the error variance consists only of sampling error and the between-people variance consists only of the individual differences. We'll see how exactly we're able to quantify these different sources in a moment. -->

With independent samples, we could happen to put more fast children in one condition than another. With repeated measures, each condition contains exactly the same children. Their stable differences in overall speed can't push one condition's mean above another's.

But those differences still contribute to the within-groups sum of squares. In the second stage of the partition, we separate them out, leaving a much smaller error term for $F$. We split within-groups variability into two components: **between-people variability**, how much the children's overall levels differ, and **error**, what's left after setting those differences aside.

What's left isn't just inaccurate measurement. Children might respond differently to practice or competition, or have a particularly good or bad trial. Those departures from the average pattern remain in the error component.

{{< interactive-figure relatedPartitionDiagram makeVariancePartitionDiagram options='{"preset":"related","formula":false,"ariaLabel":"Diagram partitioning total variability into variance between groups, which contains any treatment effect plus remaining chance, and variance within groups, which contains remaining chance and individual differences and is further partitioned into variance between people, which contains individual differences, and error variance, which contains the remaining chance."}' fallback="Diagram partitioning total variability into variance between groups, which contains any treatment effect plus remaining chance, and variance within groups, which contains remaining chance and individual differences and is further partitioned into variance between people, which contains individual differences, and error variance, which contains the remaining chance." >}}

### A modified $F$ ratio

We will still use the same numerator, $MS_{\text{between}}$, but we're going to use a different denominator for the $F$ ratio: $MS_{\text{error}}$. Under the null hypothesis, both estimate the same remaining variance. A difference between the population means can make the numerator larger, just as before.

Let's see how we separate out the people component using the children's actual scores. So far we've grouped scores by condition; now we'll also group them by the child they belong to.

::::: {#act-related-partition .callout-tip .interactive}

Regroup the scores into one row per child. Instead of comparing condition means, we're going to compare the children's means.

Find each child's average across the three conditions. The outlines show where their scores would be if all three equaled that child's mean. The actual scores stay where they were.

How far is each child's mean from the grand mean? That's the deviation we need to quantify differences in their overall speed.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Squares" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"squares","animate":true}'}
Square each deviation. Larger squares represent children whose overall times were farther from the grand mean, whether faster or slower.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="people" data-major-title="People" data-title="Sum" data-action='{"stage":"people","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
Each child's mean represents three scores, so count each square three times. They add up to $SS_{\text{people}} = 601.33$, part of the within-groups variability we already counted.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Centred" data-title="Centre" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"shift","animate":true}'}
Now shift each child's three scores together until their mean lines up with the grand mean. These outlines are adjusted scores, not times the children actually ran. We've removed their differences in overall speed, but kept the gaps between each child's scores.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Centred" data-title="Lanes" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"lanes","animate":true}'}
Put the adjusted scores back into their condition rows. The condition means are unchanged, but the spread around them is much smaller: the children no longer differ in overall speed.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Centred" data-title="What's left" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"squares","animate":true}'}
Measure each adjusted score's deviation from its condition mean and square it. This is the variability that remains after accounting for both the conditions and the children's overall levels.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="centre" data-major-title="Centred" data-title="Error" data-action='{"stage":"centre","phase":"sum","animate":true}'}
The squares fill the remaining space: $SS_{\text{error}} = 25.87$. We could get the same answer by subtracting $SS_{\text{people}}$ from $SS_{\text{within}}$.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="Partition" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"partition","animate":true}'}
The same total now has three parts: between groups, between people, and error. We haven't lost any variability; we've identified another part of it.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="Split" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"split","animate":true}'}
For $F$, we take the between-groups and error components. The people component stays behind. It still contributes to total variability, but it isn't part of the comparison between conditions.
:::

::: {.tutorial-step data-major="compare" data-major-title="Compare" data-title="F" data-action='{"stage":"compare","phase":"f","animate":true}'}
Divide each sum by its degrees of freedom, then divide the mean squares. The numerator is unchanged; the denominator now uses only error. Here $F(2, 8) = 24.14$. Next we'll work through those degrees of freedom and calculations.
:::
::::

:::::

The adjustment in the tutorial is called **centering**. We subtract each child's mean and add the grand mean: $X - M_{\text{person}} + M_{\text{grand}}$. Stephen's mean is 1.33 seconds above the grand mean, so we subtract 1.33 from each of his times. His first time, 51 seconds, becomes 49.67. All three of Stephen's scores move by the same amount; their differences stay the same. After doing this for every child, the condition means stay the same too. We've taken out overall speed without taking out the differences we're interested in.

## Sums of squares and degrees of freedom

So here's how we calculate this modified $F$ ratio for related-samples data. These formulas assume a complete set of scores: each person contributes one score in every condition. If someone misses a condition, we can't simply leave that cell blank and carry on with the same calculation.

We start with the sums of squares and degrees of freedom. And the total, between-groups, and within-groups components are exactly the same as they were for the independent-samples designs.

Then we get to the two new components for between-people and error variability. The equation[^related-computational] for between people has the same form as $SS_{\text{between}}$, with person means in place of group means:

$$ SS_{\text{people}} = \Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 $$

$M_{\text{person}}$ is the mean of one person's scores across the conditions. We square each person's deviation from the grand mean and multiply by $k$, the number of conditions, since each person's mean represents $k$ scores. Then we add them up. It's the same idea as between groups, just regrouping the scores by person.

The final component, and the one that will become our denominator, is what's left. Anything left over after taking the individual-difference variability out of within-groups variability is the error variability, so we can find it by subtraction:

$$ SS_{\text{error}} = SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}} $$

Or we can get the same answer directly, from each score's deviation from its group mean once that person's overall deviation from the grand mean has been taken out: $SS_{\text{error}} = \Sigma (X - M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{group}} + M_{\text{grand}})^2$.

The two new components have degrees of freedom of their own. For $SS_{\text{people}}$, we computed the deviation of each person's mean from the grand mean. So that's $n$ means, deviating from a single grand mean, and $df_{\text{people}} = n - 1$, the number of people minus one. (Since everyone contributes one score to each condition, $n$ is also the number of scores in each condition.)[^related-matched] The error degrees of freedom are what's left of $df_{\text{within}}$:

$$ df_{\text{error}} = df_{\text{within}} - df_{\text{people}} = (N - k) - (n - 1) = (k - 1)(n - 1) $$

The degrees of freedom split just like the sums of squares: some of the within-groups variability is accounted for by people, and error gets what's left.

[^related-matched]: In a matched-subjects design, we do the same calculation with matched sets in place of people. Each set contributes one score per condition, and $n$ counts sets. Other books may call the between-people component “between subjects” or “between participants.”

[^related-computational]: As in Chapter 14, there's also a computational version of this formula. It uses $P$, a participant total (the sum of the scores for one person), and $G$, the grand total.

    $$ SS_{\text{people}} = \Sigma \frac{P^2}{k} - \frac{G^2}{N} $$

    We'll stick with the definitional formula here too.

### Mean squares and $F$

Once we calculate the required sums of squares and degrees of freedom, the rest is easy. We calculate the mean squares by dividing each relevant sum of squares by its degrees of freedom. Then we divide the numerator by the denominator. The numerator is the same as before; we just have to remember to use $MS_{\text{error}}$ in the denominator:

$$
\begin{align}
MS_{\text{between}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}} \\
MS_{\text{error}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}}
\end{align}
$$

$$ F = \frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}} $$

And the interpretation of the $F$ ratio is exactly the same. A large numerator relative to the denominator is evidence against the null hypothesis. Setting aside differences between people can make the denominator smaller, giving us a more powerful test. It isn't guaranteed, though: we also lose degrees of freedom. We'll come back to that tradeoff at the end.

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-partitioning-variance.qmd >}}

## A related-samples ANOVA, step by step

So let's run through the hypothesis test for the five children in @tbl-related-anova-data. We'll concentrate on what's different from Chapter 14.

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

As always, we start that hypothesis test by stating our hypotheses. The null here is that the population mean time is the same in all three conditions — that $\mu_{\text{first alone}} = \mu_{\text{second alone}} = \mu_{\text{competition}}$. The alternative hypothesis is that at least one condition differs from at least one other.

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

Step two is to determine the critical value for the test, with $\alpha = .05$. We use the same $F$ table as before, with the degrees of freedom for our numerator and new denominator:

$$df_{\text{between}} = k - 1 = 2 \qquad df_{\text{error}} = (k - 1)(n - 1) = 2(4) = 8$$

In @tbl-related-anova-critical, the column for 2 and the row for 8 give a critical $F$ of 4.46.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-critical}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaCriticalTable makeFTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the competition test","alpha":0.05,"df1":{"from":1,"to":4},"df2":{"from":6,"to":10},"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"df1":2,"df2":8,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="F table excerpt for numerator df 1 through 4 and denominator df 6 through 10, highlighting the .05 critical value of 4.46 at F(2, 8)." >}}

An excerpt of the $F$ table, with the critical value for $df = 2$ and $8$ highlighted.
:::

If these 15 scores had come from independent samples, the denominator would have had 12 degrees of freedom and the critical value would have been 3.89. Our lower degrees of freedom mean we need a more extreme $F$ to reject the null, just as we saw with the related-samples $t$ test.

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-degrees-of-freedom.qmd >}}

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

Step three is to calculate the $F$ ratio for the data. Like the calculations for the independent-samples ANOVA, this is a little labor intensive. But it's worth practicing to make sure you understand how to use each equation and what each component represents.

It's a good idea to use a summary table as you work through this by hand. It's the same as we used in Chapter 14; it just has additional rows for new sources of variance: between people and error. @tbl-related-anova-summary-blank shows the equations for each element.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-summary-blank .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Between groups | $\Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $k - 1$ | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}}$ | $\dfrac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}}$ |
| Within groups | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2$ | $N - k$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Between people | $\Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $n - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Error | $SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}}$ | $(k - 1)(n - 1)$ | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}}$ | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | $\Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2$ | $N - 1$ | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

A related-samples ANOVA summary table, showing each equation.
:::

To save you some trouble, @tbl-related-anova-data gives each condition's mean and sum of squares. Here are $n$, $k$, $N$, and $M_{\text{grand}}$ too. Remember that we have five children but 15 scores. You're welcome to check my math.

$$n = 5 \qquad k = 3 \qquad N = 15 \qquad M_{\text{grand}} = 46.67$$

The only new component we need to calculate is $SS_{\text{people}}$, since we can then find error by subtraction. But let's also see how one of those error squares comes from an individual score. In the tutorial, Stephen's first time went from 51 to 49.67 seconds after we removed his difference in overall speed. The first-alone mean stayed at 50.20. So his adjusted score is $49.67 - 50.20 = -0.53$ seconds from that condition's mean. This remaining deviation is called a **residual**; squaring it gives about 0.28.

That's what the longer expression in @tbl-related-anova-people does: $X - M_{\text{person}} + M_{\text{grand}}$ adjusts the score, and subtracting $M_{\text{group}}$ gives the residual. The table shows both the people squares and these error squares for every score. Notice that each child's people square appears three times, once per condition. That's why the equation multiplies by $k$. The error squares vary from score to score; their sum is the same as we get by subtracting the people component from within groups.

Here's the full working, so you can check your answers:

$$
\begin{align}
SS_{\text{total}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{grand}})^2 = 783.33 \\
SS_{\text{within}} &= \Sigma (X - M_{\text{group}})^2 \\ &= 272.80 + 201.20 + 153.20 = 627.20 \\
SS_{\text{between}} &= \Sigma n_{\text{group}}(M_{\text{group}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\ &= 5(3.53)^2 + 5(0.73)^2 + 5(-4.27)^2 = 156.13 \\
SS_{\text{people}} &= \Sigma k(M_{\text{person}} - M_{\text{grand}})^2 \\ &= 5.33 + 75.00 + 56.33 + 456.33 + 8.33 = 601.33 \\
SS_{\text{error}} &= SS_{\text{within}} - SS_{\text{people}} \approx 627.20 - 601.33 \approx 25.87
\end{align}
$$

$$
\begin{align}
df_{\text{total}} &= N - 1 = 15 - 1 = 14 \\
df_{\text{within}} &= N - k = 15 - 3 = 12 \\
df_{\text{between}} &= k - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2 \\
df_{\text{people}} &= n - 1 = 5 - 1 = 4 \\
df_{\text{error}} &= (k - 1)(n - 1) = (3 - 1)(5 - 1) = 8
\end{align}
$$

$$
\begin{align}
MS_{\text{between}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}} = \frac{156.13}{2} = 78.07 \\
MS_{\text{error}} &= \frac{SS_{\text{error}}}{df_{\text{error}}} = \frac{25.87}{8} = 3.23
\end{align}
$$

$$ F = \frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{error}}} = \frac{78.07}{3.23} \approx 24.14 $$

And here's the completed summary table:

::: {#tbl-related-anova-summary .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Between groups | 156.13 | 2 | 78.07 | 24.14 |
| Within groups | 627.20 | 12 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Between people | 601.33 | 4 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |
| &emsp;Error | 25.87 | 8 | 3.23 | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | 783.33 | 14 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

Completed related-samples ANOVA summary table for the competition example.
:::

### Step 4: Make a decision

So now we've calculated our $F$ ratio, we're ready to make our decision. We compare it to the critical value we figured out from the table, and if our $F$ ratio is bigger than the critical value, we reject the null hypothesis. So here with our $F$ of 24.14, well beyond the critical value of 4.46, we can comfortably reject the null. There is a significant difference among our three conditions. The corresponding $p$-value is about $.0004$, so $p$ is less than $\alpha$.

::: {#fig-related-anova-decision}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"f","df1":2,"df2":8,"title":"Null distribution: F(2, 8)","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[0,27],"xTicks":6,"labels":{"x":"F ratio"},"shade":{"tail":"right","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":4.45897,"label":"4.46","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":24.14433,"label":"F = 24.14","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null F distribution with 2 and 8 degrees of freedom. The rejection region lies above 4.46; the observed F of 24.14 is far into the rejection region." >}}

The observed $F = 24.14$ falls beyond the critical value of the null $F$ distribution with $df = 2$ and $8$.
:::

{{< include quizzes/15-related-anova-calculate-f.qmd >}}

### Step 5: Estimate the effect, compare the conditions, and consider power

#### Effect size: partial $\eta^2$

In Chapter 14 we used $\eta^2$, the between-groups sum of squares as a proportion of the total. Here we'll use **partial eta squared**, $\eta^2_p$. It asks what proportion is between groups once we've set aside the between-people component.

Think of the bucket again. Leave the people layer behind, and the remaining total is $SS_{\text{between}} + SS_{\text{error}}$. That's the same as $SS_{\text{total}} - SS_{\text{people}}$. So:

$$\eta^2_p = \frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{SS_{\text{between}} + SS_{\text{error}}} = \frac{156.13}{156.13 + 25.87} = .86$$

About 86% of that remaining variability is between conditions. Ordinary $\eta^2$ would still be possible, but would give a different answer, $.20$, because it includes the large people component in the denominator. So be careful comparing effect sizes: the partial and ordinary versions describe different shares of the data's variability.

#### Post-hoc tests

The ANOVA tells us the population means aren't all equal, but not which ones differ. We can follow it with Tukey's HSD, as in Chapter 14, protecting our experimentwise $\alpha$ while comparing all three pairs.

The procedure is the same, but we use $MS_{\text{error}}$ and its degrees of freedom. In @tbl-related-anova-q, find the column for three conditions and the row for $df_{\text{error}} = 8$. Their intersection gives the critical studentized range value, $q = 4.04$, for $\alpha = .05$.

::: {#tbl-related-anova-q}
{{< interactive-figure relatedAnovaTukeyTable makeTukeyTable options='{"title":"Tukey critical values for the competition test","alpha":0.05,"k":{"from":2,"to":6},"df":{"from":4,"to":10},"tableMinWidth":"0","cellMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"36rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"k":3,"df":8,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="Studentized range critical values at alpha .05 for 2 through 6 conditions and error df 4 through 10. The highlighted cell for 3 conditions and 8 error degrees of freedom is q = 4.04." >}}

Critical values of $q$ for $\alpha = .05$. The column gives the number of conditions; the row gives the error degrees of freedom.
:::

And $n = 5$, the number of scores in each condition:

$$HSD = q \sqrt{\frac{MS_{\text{error}}}{n}} = 4.04 \sqrt{\frac{3.23}{5}} \approx 3.25$$

Any difference between means greater than 3.25 seconds is significant at the $.05$ level. This pooled-error comparison relies on an assumption called sphericity, which we'll explain shortly.

| Comparison | Absolute difference | Exceeds 3.25 seconds? |
|:--|--:|:--:|
| First alone vs. second alone | 2.80 seconds | No |
| Second alone vs. competition | 5.00 seconds | Yes |
| First alone vs. competition | 7.80 seconds | Yes |

The two gaps involving competition exceed the HSD, but the gap between the solo trials doesn't. The children improved by an average of 2.80 seconds before competing, and by another 5.00 seconds when competition began. Only the comparisons involving competition are significant.

#### Statistical power

As in Chapter 13, power depends partly on how strongly people's scores go together across conditions. If generally fast children stay fast and slow children stay slow, we can remove a lot of variability that isn't relevant to the comparison. We'll see the difference this makes in the closing example.

For planning a future study, we'd need an estimate of how variable the within-person changes are, along with the differences we want to detect. The spread of scores in each condition alone doesn't tell us that.

## Reporting and interpreting results

So finally, we're ready to report the results. As usual, you need descriptives for each condition; a statement of what test was performed and whether it was significant; the test statistic itself with degrees of freedom; $p$ compared to $\alpha$; and effect size. And here we include a summary of the post-hoc tests stating which conditions differed significantly and nonsignificantly.

> In this selected five-child example, a single-factor, related-samples ANOVA revealed a significant difference among children's times on their first race alone ($M = 50.20$, $SD = 8.26$ seconds), a second race alone ($M = 47.40$, $SD = 7.09$ seconds), and a race in competition ($M = 42.40$, $SD = 6.19$ seconds); $F(2, 8) = 24.14$, $p < .001$, $\eta^2_p = .86$. Tukey HSD comparisons indicated that children were significantly faster in competition than on either solo trial. The two solo trials did not differ significantly.

But if you graphed the condition means in the usual way, the result might look surprising. The confidence intervals in @fig-related-results overlap, even though both comparisons involving competition were significant.

::: {#fig-related-results}
{{< interactive-figure relatedResultsGraph makeGraph options='{"type":"interval","orientation":"vertical","mark":"bar","data":[{"label":"First alone","estimate":50.2,"lower":39.9459,"upper":60.4541,"color":"var(--sfs-text, #222)"},{"label":"Second alone","estimate":47.4,"lower":38.5938,"upper":56.2062,"color":"var(--sfs-text, #222)"},{"label":"Competition","estimate":42.4,"lower":34.7157,"upper":50.0843,"color":"var(--sfs-text, #222)"}],"yDomain":[0,70],"yTickValues":[0,20,40,60],"width":640,"height":380,"margin":{"top":22,"right":16,"bottom":65,"left":65},"showValues":false,"labels":{"x":"Condition","y":"Mean time (seconds)"},"ariaLabel":"Mean times: first alone 50.20 seconds, second alone 47.40, and competition 42.40. Error bars are 95 percent confidence intervals for each condition mean, calculated from its own standard deviation. All three intervals overlap."}' fallback="Mean times: first alone 50.20 seconds, second alone 47.40, and competition 42.40. Error bars are 95 percent confidence intervals for each condition mean, calculated from its own standard deviation. All three intervals overlap." >}}

A bar graph showing average times in the three conditions. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals for each condition's mean, each calculated from that condition's own standard deviation ($df = 4$).
:::

Those intervals describe uncertainty about each condition's mean separately. They still reflect how much the children differ from one another. They don't show how consistently each child's time changed.

@fig-related-profiles makes that visible. Each line follows one child across the conditions. Every line falls at both steps, even though the children start at quite different levels. The graph follows the order in which all five children experienced the conditions.

::: {#fig-related-profiles}
{{< interactive-figure relatedProfileLines makeProfileLines options='{"categories":["First alone","Second alone","Competition"],"series":[{"name":"Stephen","color":0,"values":[51,50,43]},{"name":"Mary W.","color":3,"values":[56,53,46]},{"name":"Bertha","color":7,"values":[56,49,48]},{"name":"Clyde","color":1,"values":[36,35,32]},{"name":"Lucile","color":5,"values":[52,50,43]}],"yDomain":[30,60],"yLabel":"Time (seconds)","xLabel":"Condition","ariaLabel":"One line per child across the three conditions. Every line falls from first alone to second alone and again to competition, and the lines stay in much the same order."}' fallback="One line per child across the three conditions. Every line falls at each step." >}}

The same data, with one line for each child.
:::

To put confidence intervals around the changes themselves, we can use the difference scores for each pair of conditions, just as in Chapter 13. Now the differences in overall speed are out of the picture. The interval for the solo-to-solo change in @fig-related-differences includes zero; the two involving competition don't. These are ordinary 95% paired intervals, though, not adjusted for multiple comparisons like Tukey's test. They also use each pair's own variability rather than the pooled error term, so they needn't always agree with Tukey's decisions.

For example, subtracting each child's second-alone time from their competition time gives differences of $-7$, $-7$, $-1$, $-3$, and $-7$ seconds. Their mean is $M_D = -5.00$ and their standard deviation is $s_D = \sqrt{8} = 2.83$. With five children, the standard error is $s_{M_D} = s_D/\sqrt{n} = 1.26$ seconds. Using the two-tailed critical $t = 2.776$ for $df = 4$, the 95% interval is:

$$M_D \pm t_{\text{critical}}s_{M_D} = -5.00 \pm 2.776\sqrt{\frac{8}{5}} \approx [-8.51, -1.49]$$

The calculation uses unrounded values. Both limits are negative: the interval runs from a decrease of 8.51 seconds to a decrease of 1.49 seconds.

::: {#fig-related-differences}
{{< interactive-figure relatedDifferencesGraph makeGraph options='{"type":"interval","orientation":"horizontal","data":[{"label":"First to second alone","estimate":-2.8,"lower":-5.8917,"upper":0.2917},{"label":"Second to competition","estimate":-5,"lower":-8.512,"upper":-1.488},{"label":"First to competition","estimate":-7.8,"lower":-10.6314,"upper":-4.9686}],"xDomain":[-12,2],"xTickValues":[-12,-8,-4,0],"reference":0,"margin":{"left":164},"width":640,"height":240,"showValues":false,"labels":{"x":"Mean change in time (seconds)"},"ariaLabel":"Mean changes with 95 percent confidence intervals: first to second alone, minus 2.80 seconds, from minus 5.89 to 0.29; second alone to competition, minus 5.00, from minus 8.51 to minus 1.49; first alone to competition, minus 7.80, from minus 10.63 to minus 4.97. Only the solo-to-solo interval includes zero."}' fallback="Mean changes with 95 percent confidence intervals: first to second alone, minus 2.80 seconds, from minus 5.89 to 0.29; second alone to competition, minus 5.00, from minus 8.51 to minus 1.49; first alone to competition, minus 7.80, from minus 10.63 to minus 4.97. Only the solo-to-solo interval includes zero." >}}

95% confidence intervals for the mean change between each pair of conditions, calculated from each pair's difference scores as in @fig-related-ci. These intervals aren't adjusted for multiple comparisons.
:::

### Interpreting the results

The larger improvement when competition began fits the idea that a rival helped the children speed up. But a nonsignificant solo-to-solo comparison doesn't mean practice had no effect. And a significant change after a nonsignificant one doesn't establish that the two changes differ. The times suggest a story; the tests haven't proved that story.

There's also the order problem. Both solo trials came before any competition, so their difference can't reflect a lingering effect of racing against someone. But competition always came third. We don't know how fast these children would have gone on a third trial alone. Further practice could explain some or all of the improvement we attributed to competition.

Triplett varied the order across children, as we saw in Chapter 13. Including both orders would help keep competition from always benefiting from coming later, though competing might itself affect a subsequent solo trial [@triplett1898dynamogenic]. We've used just one order to keep the worked example easy to follow; that makes its causal interpretation more limited.

Finally, these are five deliberately selected children from the part of Triplett's table labeled “stimulated positively.” Across all 20 children who followed this same order, the first-to-second-alone improvement averages 3.36 seconds, and the next improvement, when competition begins, 2.47 seconds. Our five make a particular pattern easy to see; they don't establish its size or significance in the wider population. As usual, the design and the selection of data matter as much as the calculation.

### Assumptions

The same basic considerations apply as before, with some changes for related samples. We expect scores from the same child to be related; different children's responses should be independent of one another. And as with the related-samples $t$ test, normality concerns the within-person differences we're analyzing, rather than simply the scores in each condition.

With three or more conditions, we also need **sphericity**: the population variances of the difference scores should be the same for every pair of conditions. This is different from Chapter 14's homogeneity of variance assumption: here we're comparing the variances of the *differences*, rather than the variances of the scores in each condition. Put concretely, children's first-to-second-alone changes should be about as variable as their second-alone-to-competition changes and their first-alone-to-competition changes. We're using one pooled error term for all those comparisons, so it needs to represent them reasonably well.

Our five children's difference variances are 6.2 for first to second alone, 8.0 for second alone to competition, and 5.2 for first alone to competition. Those are fairly similar. When sphericity doesn't hold, the usual test can reject the null too often. Software can apply a correction, such as Greenhouse–Geisser, which adjusts the degrees of freedom and $p$-value without changing $F$ itself.[^related-sphericity] With only two conditions, there's just one set of difference scores, so sphericity isn't an issue.

[^related-sphericity]: Software often provides Mauchly's test of sphericity, though a nonsignificant result doesn't guarantee the assumption holds, especially with a small sample. Greenhouse–Geisser uses a value called epsilon to adjust the degrees of freedom; values near 1 indicate little adjustment. Here epsilon is $.94$ and the corrected $p$ is about $.0006$, so the decision is unchanged. Follow-up comparisons also need an appropriate method if sphericity is doubtful.

## Back to two conditions

To finish, let's return to the five children and two conditions from Chapter 13, in @tbl-triplett. We analyzed those times with a related-samples $t$ test, and then saw what would happen if we ignored the pairs and used an independent-samples test. What happens if we use ANOVA instead?

Just what you might expect after Chapter 14: $F = t^2$. Ignoring the pairs gives $F(1, 8) = 0.97$, the square of the independent-samples $t$ before rounding. Using the pairs gives $F(1, 4) = 8.47$, the square of our related-samples $t$. Each has the same $p$-value as its corresponding two-tailed $t$ test. We're expressing the same evidence in a different way, not getting a second confirmation of it.

### The advantages of treating scores as related

Compare the first two columns of @tbl-related-analyses. The condition means haven't changed, so neither has the numerator. But almost all the within-groups variability turns out to be between children. Taking it out leaves a much smaller error component. Even after allowing for the lost degrees of freedom, the denominator falls from 99 to 11.35, and $F$ grows from 0.97 to 8.47.

The two approaches remove the same differences in overall speed. The $t$ test does it by subtracting each child's two times; ANOVA identifies a separate people component. With two conditions, its error sum of squares is exactly half the sum of squares of the difference scores: $90.8/2 = 45.4$.

| | Ignoring the pairs | Using the pairs | Pairs scrambled |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| $SS_{\text{between}}$ | 96.10 | 96.10 | 96.10 |
| $SS_{\text{within}}$ | 792.00 | 792.00 | 792.00 |
| $SS_{\text{people}}$ | | 746.60 | 397.60 |
| $SS$ in the denominator | 792.00 | 45.40 | 394.40 |
| $df$ in the denominator | 8 | 4 | 4 |
| $MS$ in the denominator | 99.00 | 11.35 | 98.60 |
| Critical $F$ | 5.32 | 7.71 | 7.71 |
| $F$ | 0.97 | 8.47 | 0.97 |
| $t$ | $-0.99$ | $-2.91$ | $-0.99$ |
| $p$ | .353 | .044 | .379 |

: The same scores analyzed three ways. The independent-samples calculation ignores the known pairing; the scrambled pairs are artificial. {#tbl-related-analyses}

### What if scores aren't related?

Why does using the pairs help so much here? Because the children's scores go together: a child who was fast alone tended to be fast in competition too. If their scores didn't go together, there would be much less to gain.

Let's deliberately scramble the competition times, as in @tbl-related-scrambled. These aren't real pairings anymore. But each column still contains exactly the same scores, so its mean and spread haven't changed. Anything the independent-samples calculation can see is unchanged.

| Child | Alone | Competition |
|:------|--:|--:|
| A | 54 | 57 |
| B | 67 | 36 |
| C | 38 | 39 |
| D | 46 | 43 |
| E | 42 | 41 |
| $M$ | 49.4 | 43.2 |

: The times from Chapter 13, with the competition column scrambled so that the two columns no longer go together. {#tbl-related-scrambled}

Now look at the last column of @tbl-related-analyses. The people sum of squares is much smaller. It isn't zero: even randomly grouped scores have different averages. But once we've divided by the new degrees of freedom, $MS_{\text{error}} = 98.60$, almost the same as the original $MS_{\text{within}} = 99$. Our $F$ is back to about 0.97, while the critical value is still higher because of the lower degrees of freedom.

@fig-related-buckets shows the two partitions. With the real pairs, the people layer takes up most of the within-groups variability. With scrambled pairs, it leaves much more error behind.

::: {#fig-related-buckets}
{{< interactive-figure relatedBucketReal makeAnovaVariabilityExplorer options='{"stage":"compare","phase":"f","scores":false,"calculations":true,"controlsOpen":false,"groups":[{"name":"Alone","values":[54,67,38,46,42]},{"name":"Competition","values":[43,57,39,41,36]}],"people":["Child A","Child B","Child C","Child D","Child E"],"axisLabel":"Time (seconds)","xMin":30,"xMax":72}' fallback="The partition for Chapter 13's five children: a thick between-people layer stays in the total, leaving a thin error layer, so the between-groups mean square is far larger than the error mean square." >}}

{{< interactive-figure relatedBucketScrambled makeAnovaVariabilityExplorer options='{"stage":"compare","phase":"f","scores":false,"calculations":true,"controlsOpen":false,"groups":[{"name":"Alone","values":[54,67,38,46,42]},{"name":"Competition","values":[57,36,39,43,41]}],"people":["Child A","Child B","Child C","Child D","Child E"],"axisLabel":"Time (seconds)","xMin":30,"xMax":72}' fallback="The partition for the scrambled scores: the same total and between-groups layers, but a much thinner between-people layer, leaving a thick error layer, so the two mean squares are about the same size." >}}

The real pairs (top) and the scrambled pairs (bottom).
:::

So a related-samples design doesn't automatically make a test more powerful. It helps when the related scores tend to go together, reducing the relevant variability enough to compensate for the lost degrees of freedom. And as in Chapter 13, this isn't an invitation to try both analyses and keep the result we prefer. The design tells us which calculation is appropriate; the comparison shows why that matters.
